---
title: "10 · Hazard integration"
---

The point of the twin is the handoff: delivering the coupled subsurface state to the models that
turn it into flood, landslide, and liquefaction hazard — on the shared 90 m grid, with per-cell
uncertainty, and with a clean division of labour so this repository owns the *dynamic* state and the
downstream data-prep owns the *static* stack.

## The digital-twin MVP

The pieces compose into an uncertainty-aware, 90 m, co-located estimate that evolves as data are
assimilated: one hydrologic year at 5-day cadence, with the state (groundwater depth-to-water, soil
moisture, Vs30) on top and the matching per-cell 1σ below. In the MVP the time evolution comes from a
physically realistic synthetic dv/v assimilated onto the real static fields, so the animation shows the
assimilation *machinery* at work — the state updates and σ shrinks where and when sensors constrain it
— and the same operators run on measured dv/v once the multi-year waveform run lands.

## LandLab landslide coupling (dynamic export)

The complementary downstream consumer is the **LandLab** landslide chain (the infinite-slope
`LandslideProbability` Factor of Safety). The interface is clean because the two repositories own
different halves of the input stack:

- `landslide-data-prep` owns the **static stack** (DEM, SOLUS soil, NLCD → cohesion/φ/LAI);
- this twin owns the **dynamic hydrological state** and exports only those fields, on the same grid.

`src.io.landlab_export` writes `water_table__depth` (mean and seasonal-high), `soil_moisture__saturation_fraction`,
and `soil_water__recharge_rate` in the DataHub canonical vocabulary as LandLab-ready ESRI ASCII (`.asc`)
+ COG + a provenance manifest, with per-cell σ and the confidence mask applied. The *static*
soil-hydromechanical parameters that both sides need — chiefly $K_{sat}$ and soil thickness — are held
to one shared pedotransfer through the modular registry (`src.models.soil_hydraulics`), so our water
budget and LandLab's transmissivity stay consistent.

::: {.callout-important}
## What slope stability consumes is pore pressure, not depth to water
The mechanically fundamental variable for shallow landsliding is the **pore-water pressure at or near
the failure surface**, entering through Terzaghi effective stress $\sigma' = \sigma - u$
[@bogaard2016landslidehydrology]. Depth to water table is an *upstream proxy*: it becomes a pore
pressure only under a stated hydrologic assumption, and the assumptions are not equivalent.

- Under a **hydrostatic** column, $u(z) = \rho_w g\,(h_{wt}-z)$.
- Under **slope-parallel** flow — which is what an infinite-slope factor of safety implicitly assumes
  — $u(z) = \rho_w g\,(h_{wt}-z)\cos^2\beta$, i.e. 25% smaller at $30^\circ$.
- Under **transient infiltration**, neither holds: a wetting front can raise $u$ at a failure surface
  well before any regional water table moves, and excess pore pressure can be generated by processes
  the water table does not see at all [@pelascini2022hillslope].

`src/models/hydro_state.py` therefore provides
`pore_pressure_hydrostatic_below_water_table()` and `pore_pressure_slope_parallel()` as two
**separately named** functions, and deliberately does *not* offer a generic `pore_pressure_from_head`
— a generic helper would let a slope-stability caller inherit a hydrologic condition it never chose.
This is also why #130's distinction matters mechanically and not only semantically: a **shallow
perched or transient saturated zone** on a hillslope, the **regional phreatic water table**, and a
**deeper confined hydraulic head** are three different things, and it is usually the first that
triggers a shallow failure while the twin's well network mostly sees the second. Collapsing them into
one generic "GWL" would put the wrong pressure on the failure plane.

The export contract is unchanged — LandLab's `LandslideProbability` takes `water_table__depth` and
forms its own relative wetness — but the DTW we ship should be read as a *derived hydrologic input
under stated assumptions*, not as the mechanical driver itself. #127/#128 own closing that gap.
:::

## Liquefaction: seasonal-high depth to water, and Vs30 → NEHRP site-class probability

For liquefaction the situation is the reverse of landsliding: **water-table depth is itself a
first-class predictor**, not a proxy for one. The updated global geospatial liquefaction model of
@zhu2017geospatial takes *modeled* water-table depth as an explicit input alongside $V_{S30}$,
topographic and climatic terms, and it is one of the model's important predictors — which is exactly
why a dynamic, seasonal water table is worth producing rather than a static climatology
(#139/#141/#142). The relevant epoch is the **seasonal high** (the shallow tail of DTW,
`seasonal_high_water_table()`), because that is when a given ground motion is most likely to
liquefy the deposit.

Two constraints follow for calibration, and they are the substance of #142. First, the target is the
shallow unconfined table in liquefiable units, so it must be calibrated against wells that actually
sample it: a confined or deep piezometric head used as "DTW truth" would bias the seasonal high by
tens of metres in the wrong direction, and the observation semantics of
[the assimilation chapter](04-assimilation.qmd#which-wells-actually-observe-the-water-table) exist to
prevent that. Second, the accuracy target is sub-metre in the top few metres, which is a far harder
ask than the domain-wide block-CV RMSE reported in
[state evaluation](05-state-evaluation.qmd) and must be reported separately for the liquefiable
lowland rather than inherited from the pooled score.

### Vs30 → NEHRP site-class probability

The Vs30 estimate is drawn preferentially from the measurement-based **Soil Velocity Model**
[@grant2025svm] where staged, with the Wald–Allen slope proxy as the always-available fallback (see
[Structural model](00-structural-model.qmd)). For the Sanger liquefaction GLM, the near-surface
stiffness is delivered not as a raw Vs30 with a percent σ but as a **NEHRP/ASCE-7 site-class
probability**: `src.data.fetch_vs30.nehrp_class_probabilities`
integrates the Vs30 estimate and its 1σ over the class boundaries (180 / 360 / 760 / 1500 m s⁻¹) to
return $P(\text{E},\text{D},\text{C},\text{B},\text{A})$ per cell, and by differencing the CDF, the
probability of crossing any design boundary. A cell near a boundary honestly splits its mass across two
classes rather than being forced into one — the quantity a design engineer acts on.

## Flood antecedent state

For compound-flood models, the twin supplies the **antecedent hydrologic state** — how full the
subsurface stores already are when a storm arrives. A water table raised by a preceding
atmospheric-river sequence turns the next event into runoff faster; the [forecast](06-forecast.qmd)
path delivers that antecedent state ahead of the event, while a surface routing/hydrograph model (out
of scope here, #55) converts it into flood depth.
